papers.title_in_file: Quantum Computing Cost 2026: Verified Cloud QPU Pricing & Calculator
papers.what_it_is: A single-author price-reference web page (Digital Signet, dated 3 June 2026, rows re-verified 2026-09-07) that tabulates cloud QPU access prices and physical machine purchase prices.

assertions.value: The authors report that every row was re-verified on 2026-09-07: 17 of 20 entries are verified against the provider's primary pricing page, 2 are quote-only (Google Willow, D-Wave commercial Leap), and 1 (IonQ Aria on AWS Braket) has been withdrawn by its cloud and is kept as a historical reference rather than a price.
quotes: Every row was re-verified on 2026-09-07: 17 of 20 entries are verified against the provider's primary pricing page
2 are quote-only (Google Willow, D-Wave commercial Leap); 1 has been withdrawn by its cloud (IonQ Aria on AWS Braket) and is kept as a historical reference rather than a price
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope and verification status of its own inventory in the abstract.
assertions.reader_inference: The 17, 2 and 1 sum to 20. Table 1 lists 20 rows, so the count agrees with the inventory.

assertions.value: The authors state that three pricing paradigms coexist: per-shot models (AWS Braket), per-minute models (IBM Quantum) and per-program models (Azure Quantum), and that a headline shot rate cannot be compared meaningfully across Braket and Azure without computing the representative circuit.
quotes: Three pricing paradigms coexist.
Per-shot models (AWS Braket across all providers) charge a flat task fee plus a per-shot fee
Per-minute models (IBM Quantum) charge for QPU runtime in seconds
a headline shot rate cannot be compared meaningfully across Braket and Azure without computing the representative circuit
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's framing of the market; no evidence beyond the rate tables.

assertions.value: The authors state that Azure Quantum per-program pricing (which they label the AQT formula) charges a minimum per execution plus separate fees for one-qubit and two-qubit gate shots, and that the minimum-charge floors are load-bearing in cost estimation.
quotes: Per-program models (Azure Quantum AQT formula) charge a minimum per execution plus separate fees for one-qubit and two-qubit gate shots, making minimum-charge floors load-bearing in cost estimation
assertions.certainty_reason: The formula is described but its fee values are not given in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The text calls the Azure formula the AQT formula, yet Table 1 lists the Azure per-program rows under IonQ. The label is not explained. The per-gate fee values are not stated, so the formula cannot be reproduced from this page.

assertions.value: The authors report that every QPU task on AWS Braket costs $0.30, plus a per-shot rate set by the device: Rigetti Cepheus $0.000425, IQM Garnet $0.00145, IQM Emerald $0.00160, QuEra Aquila $0.01000, AQT IBEX-Q1 $0.02350, IonQ Forte $0.08000, verified at aws.amazon.com/braket/pricing on 7 September 2026.
assertions.anchor: Section 8 FAQ (How much does AWS Braket cost) and Table 2, Section 3
quotes: Every QPU task on AWS Braket costs $0.30, plus a per-shot rate set by the device: Rigetti Cepheus $0.000425, IQM Garnet $0.00145, IQM Emerald $0.00160, QuEra Aquila $0.01000, AQT IBEX-Q1 $0.02350, IonQ Forte $0.08000.
Verified at aws.amazon.com/braket/pricing on 7 September 2026.
assertions.certainty_reason: A list price the page reports from the provider's pricing page; time-sensitive and not independently checked here.
assertions.reader_inference: Prices are a snapshot as of 7 September 2026.

assertions.value: The authors report that a 10,000-shot circuit costs about $4.55 on Rigetti Cepheus and about $800.30 on IonQ Forte, and that the 10,000-shot column is their own arithmetic: the $0.30 task fee plus 10,000 x the per-shot price.
quotes: A 10,000-shot circuit is about $4.55 on Rigetti Cepheus and about $800.30 on IonQ Forte
The 10,000-shot column is our arithmetic over those rates: $0.30 task fee plus 10,000 x the per-shot price, so you can redo it.
assertions.certainty_reason: Arithmetic over cited list prices; it inherits the price risk.
assertions.reader_inference: Checked: 0.30 + 10,000 x 0.000425 = 4.55 and 0.30 + 10,000 x 0.08 = 800.30. The other Table 2 rows (14.80, 16.30, 100.30, 235.30) also follow from the stated formula.

assertions.value: The authors state that the spread across Braket devices is more than 180x per shot, so device choice, not shot count, sets a Braket bill. The paper's first section also gives a ratio of more than 175x between a 10,000-shot IonQ Forte circuit (approximately $800) and the equivalent Rigetti Cepheus circuit (approximately $5), which it attributes mainly to per-shot price differences across qubit technologies.
quotes: The spread across devices is more than 180x per shot, so device choice, not shot count, is what actually sets a Braket bill.
making a 10,000-shot IonQ Forte circuit cost approximately $800 and the equivalent Rigetti Cepheus circuit approximately $5
a ratio of more than 175×, driven primarily by per-shot pricing differences across qubit technologies
assertions.certainty_reason: A ratio computed from cited list prices.
assertions.reader_inference: 0.08 / 0.000425 is about 188, and 800.30 / 4.55 is about 176. Both of the page's thresholds hold, because they refer to the per-shot ratio and to the 10,000-shot ratio respectively.

assertions.value: The authors report Braket Direct dedicated-access reservation prices per hour of $4,100.00 on Rigetti Cepheus, $3,000.00 on IQM Garnet, $4,000.00 on IQM Emerald, $2,500.00 on QuEra Aquila, $4,800.00 on AQT IBEX-Q1 and $7,000.00 on IonQ Forte.
quotes: Reservation rates are Braket Direct dedicated-access hourly prices from the same page.
assertions.certainty_reason: A list price reported from the provider's page.
assertions.reader_inference: Prices are a snapshot as of 2026-09-07.

assertions.value: The authors state that an hour of reserved Rigetti Cepheus at $4,100 buys roughly 9.6 million shots at the on-demand rate, and conclude that reservations are about guaranteed uninterrupted access and scheduling, not about unit cost.
quotes: an hour of reserved Rigetti Cepheus at $4,100 buys roughly 9.6 million shots at the on-demand rate, so reservations are about guaranteed uninterrupted access and scheduling, not about unit cost
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's interpretation of the price table.
assertions.reader_inference: 4,100 / 0.000425 is about 9.65 million, so the figure ignores the $0.30 task fee, which is negligible only if the shots are sent in a few large tasks.

assertions.value: The authors report that on-demand Braket simulators bill per minute of runtime in one-millisecond increments with a three-second minimum per simulation, and that embedded simulators inside Hybrid Jobs carry no separate charge.
quotes: On-demand simulators bill per minute of runtime in one-millisecond increments with a three-second minimum per simulation; embedded simulators inside Hybrid Jobs carry no separate charge.
assertions.certainty_reason: A billing rule reported from the provider's page; no per-minute simulator rate is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The page gives no simulator price per minute, so simulator cost cannot be computed from it.

assertions.value: The authors list the Braket devices with these qubit counts: IonQ Forte 36 (trapped-ion), QuEra Aquila 256 (analog Hamiltonian simulator, Rydberg, neutral-atom), IQM Garnet 20, IQM Emerald 54, AQT IBEX-Q1 12 (trapped-ion) and Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q 108 (superconducting).
quotes: IonQ Forte (36 qubits, Yb-171+ trapped-ion) trapped-ion 36 $0.08 per shot verified primary
QuEra Aquila (analog Hamiltonian simulator, Rydberg) neutral-atom 256 $0.01 per shot verified primary
IQM Garnet (20-qubit superconducting) superconducting 20 $0.00145 per shot verified primary
IQM Emerald (54-qubit superconducting, Crystal 54) superconducting 54 $0.0016 per shot verified primary
AQT IBEX-Q1 (12-qubit trapped-ion, calcium-40) trapped-ion 12 $0.0235 per shot verified primary
Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q (12 × 9-qubit chiplets, Ankaa-class) superconducting 108 $0.000425 per shot verified primary
assertions.certainty_reason: Device specifications the page reports; a vendor-sourced value.
assertions.reader_inference: QuEra Aquila is an analog machine, so its 256 count is not comparable with gate-model qubit counts.

assertions.value: The authors report that a 100-shot pilot circuit on IonQ Forte via Braket costs $8.30 and the same circuit on Rigetti Cepheus $0.34, and that a 200,000-shot VQE optimisation, run as 200 tasks of 1,000 shots, costs $16,060 on IonQ Forte but $145 on Rigetti. All Braket figures include the $0.30 per-task fee, which the VQE rows carry 200 times.
quotes: A 100-shot pilot circuit on IonQ Forte via Braket costs $8.30; the same circuit on Rigetti Cepheus costs $0.34.
A 200,000-shot VQE optimisation, run as 200 tasks of 1,000 shots, costs $16,060 on IonQ Forte but $145 on Rigetti
All Braket figures include the $0.30/task fee; the VQE rows carry it 200 times, once per iteration.
assertions.certainty_reason: Arithmetic over cited list prices.
assertions.reader_inference: Checked: 200 x (0.30 + 1,000 x 0.08) = 16,060 and 200 x (0.30 + 1,000 x 0.000425) = 145. The paper does not say that any VQE job was actually run; these are price calculations, not measured runs. The $0.34 figure is 0.3425 rounded.

assertions.value: The authors tabulate a 100-shot circuit on IQM Garnet (Braket) at 0.45 and a 10,000-shot circuit on IQM Garnet (Braket) at 14.80 US dollars.
quotes: 100-shot circuit on IQM Garnet (Braket) 100 0.45 10,000-shot circuit on IQM Garnet (Braket) 10,000 14.80
assertions.certainty_reason: Arithmetic over cited list prices.
assertions.reader_inference: 0.30 + 100 x 0.00145 = 0.445, shown as 0.45 after rounding.

assertions.value: The authors report an Azure Quantum IonQ Aria 1 per-program minimum range of $12.42-97.5. They state that the minimum reflects the error-mitigation-on default and that the mitigation-off floor is $12.42.
quotes: IonQ Aria 1 (25-qubit trapped-ion) trapped-ion 25 $12.42-97.5 per program (minimum) verified primary
Single IonQ Aria 1 program on Azure (default mitigation on)
Azure IonQ Aria minimum reflects error-mitigation-on default; mitigation-off floor is $12.42.
assertions.certainty_reason: A list price range reported from the provider's page.
assertions.reader_inference: The mitigation-on minimum is about 7.9 times the mitigation-off floor, so the default setting sets the cost of the smallest job.

assertions.value: The authors report these Azure Quantum rates: IonQ Forte $25.79-168.2 per program (minimum), Rigetti Cepheus $0.02 per 10-ms, and Pasqal Fresnel $3,487 per QPU hour, and state that Azure's pricing doc carries a 2026-04-23 update stamp and every rate matches.
quotes: IonQ Forte 1 / Forte Enterprise 1 (36-qubit trapped-ion) trapped-ion 36 $25.79-168.2 per program (minimum) verified primary
Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q superconducting 108 $0.02 per 10-ms verified primary
Pasqal Fresnel (Orion Beta generation) neutral-atom 100 $3,487 per QPU hour verified primary
its pricing doc still carries a 2026-04-23 update stamp and every rate matches
assertions.certainty_reason: List prices reported from the provider's page.
assertions.reader_inference: The Azure Rigetti rate is metered per 10 ms of QPU time and is not convertible to a per-shot price without shot duration, which the page does not give.

assertions.value: The authors state that Pasqal Fresnel is priced in EUR (3,000/QPU-hr) and was converted at the ECB reference rate of 1.1622 USD/EUR (2026-09-04).
quotes: Pasqal Fresnel is priced in EUR (3,000/QPU-hr), converted at the ECB reference rate of 1.1622 USD/EUR (2026-09-04).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how its own table value was derived.
assertions.reader_inference: 3,000 x 1.1622 = 3,486.6, which rounds to the $3,487 in the table. The USD figure depends on the exchange rate of that day.

assertions.value: The authors report Azure Quantum Quantinuum H2 (56-qubit trapped-ion, QCCD) subscriptions at $125,000 per month (Standard) and $175,000 per month (Premium).
quotes: Quantinuum H2 (56-qubit trapped-ion, QCCD) trapped-ion 56 $125,000 per month verified primary
trapped-ion 56 $175,000 per month verified primary
assertions.certainty_reason: List prices reported from the provider's page.
assertions.reader_inference: The page does not say what the Standard and Premium tiers include, so the two cannot be compared beyond the price.

assertions.value: The authors report that IBM publishes: Open Plan free for up to 10 minutes of runtime per month; Pay-As-You-Go $96/minute with a 1-second minimum purchase; Flex from $72/minute against a 400-minute annual minimum, a $28,800 annual floor; Premium from $48/minute against a 5,200-minute annual minimum, a $249,600 annual floor; and On-Prem by quote. They state the pricing page was read directly on 2026-09-07.
assertions.anchor: Section 6; Section 8 FAQ (How much does IBM Quantum cost)
quotes: IBM publishes: Open Plan free for up to 10 minutes of runtime per month; Pay-As-You-Go $96/minute with a 1-second minimum purchase;
Flex from $72/minute against a 400-minute annual minimum, a $28,800 annual floor; Premium from $48/minute against a 5,200-minute annual minimum, a $249,600 annual floor; On-Prem by quote.
IBM's own pricing page became fetchable again and was read directly on 2026-09-07
assertions.certainty_reason: List prices reported from the provider's page.
assertions.reader_inference: 400 x 72 = 28,800 and 5,200 x 48 = 249,600, so the stated floors agree with the stated minimums and rates.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two committed IBM tiers are only cheaper above their break-even: 400 minutes at $72 equals 300 minutes at $96, so Flex loses to Pay-As-You-Go below 300 QPU-minutes a year.
quotes: The two committed tiers are only cheaper above their break-even: 400 minutes at $72 equals 300 minutes at $96, so Flex loses to Pay-As-You-Go below 300 QPU-minutes a year.
assertions.certainty_reason: Arithmetic over cited list prices; it assumes the full annual minimum is bought.
assertions.reader_inference: Both products equal $28,800. The statement covers Flex only. The Premium break-even against Pay-As-You-Go (249,600 / 96, about 2,600 minutes) is not given on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that buying a physical quantum computer costs about $8,700 for a SpinQ desktop teaching unit and about $2.85 million for a complete Rigetti Novera system, and that IBM's utility-scale on-premise systems carry no published purchase price.
assertions.anchor: Section 8 FAQ (How much does a quantum computer cost in 2026)
quotes: about $8,700 for a SpinQ desktop teaching unit, about $2.85 million for a complete Rigetti Novera system
IBM's utility-scale on-premise systems carry no published purchase price
assertions.certainty_reason: No source is given for these two purchase prices in the text read.
assertions.reader_inference: The text read carries no citation for the SpinQ and Novera figures, and its reference list has none for them.

assertions.value: The authors state that a D-Wave Advantage2 costs $20 million to buy, with the attribution (Florida Atlantic University, 2026).
assertions.anchor: Section 8 FAQ (How much does a quantum computer cost in 2026)
quotes: $20 million for a D-Wave Advantage2 (Florida Atlantic University, 2026)
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited price; the reference list does not carry the underlying source.
assertions.reader_inference: The attribution to Florida Atlantic University suggests a university purchase, but the text does not say so.

assertions.value: The authors state that almost everyone rents quantum access through the cloud, and that capital cost is the reason.
quotes: That capital cost is why almost everyone accesses quantum through the cloud instead.
Almost everyone rents.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's assertion with no usage data given.
assertions.reader_inference: No count of buyers or renters is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that Google Willow is research-access only with no published price, accessible through a competitive early-access programme selected by proposal, whose latest cohort submission deadline was 15 May 2026.
quotes: Google Willow is research-access only and carries no published price.
Google Willow is accessible through a competitive early-access programme, selected by proposal (the latest cohort's submission deadline was 15 May 2026)
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about a provider's access terms, as of the page date.

assertions.value: The authors state that production D-Wave Leap pricing has not been republished as a public list since 2023 industry coverage, so they mark it quote-only; the D-Wave Leap trial is listed at $0.
quotes: Production D-Wave Leap pricing has not been republished as a public list since 2023 industry coverage; we mark it quote-only rather than cite stale figures.
D-Wave Leap — Trial Advantage2 (Zephyr topology) annealer 4400 $0 free trial verified primary
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about a provider's price publication, as of the page date.

assertions.value: The authors state that the D-Wave annealer is included for completeness but its pricing is not directly comparable to gate-model machines.
quotes: Annealer paradigm (D-Wave) is included for completeness but pricing is not directly comparable to gate-model machines.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope limit of its own comparison table.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for shot-metered gate-model access, AWS Braket on the Rigetti Cepheus-108Q is the cheapest per-shot option at $0.000425/shot, so a 10,000-shot circuit costs about $4.55 including the $0.30 task fee, and that IBM's Open Plan is free for up to 10 minutes of QPU runtime per month.
assertions.anchor: Section 8 FAQ (What is the cheapest way to run a quantum circuit)
quotes: AWS Braket on the Rigetti Cepheus-108Q is the cheapest per-shot option at $0.000425/shot, so a 10,000-shot circuit costs about $4.55 including the $0.30 task fee.
IBM's Open Plan is free for up to 10 minutes of QPU runtime per month.
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparison over the page's own list-price table; the shot-metered scope matters.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim is limited to shot-metered gate-model access listed on this page; other providers are not covered.

assertions.value: The authors state that per-shot superconducting access (Rigetti, IBM Heron) is cheaper but operates at about 99.1-99.7% two-qubit fidelity, that trapped-ion access (IonQ, Quantinuum) operates at about 99.5-99.8% production fidelity, and that research-grade demonstrations reach 99.99% via electronic qubit control.
quotes: Per-shot superconducting access (Rigetti, IBM Heron) is cheaper but operates at ~99.1-99.7% two-qubit fidelity
trapped-ion access (IonQ, Quantinuum) operates at ~99.5-99.8% production fidelity, with research-grade demonstrations of 99.99% via electronic qubit control
assertions.certainty_reason: Reported fidelities attributed to other work; the page measured none.
assertions.reader_inference: The fidelity figures come from the vendor and press sources in the reference list (a Rigetti press release and an IonQ blog), not from an independent benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors tabulate reported two-qubit gate fidelities: Oxford Ionics (now IonQ) electronic-control gate 99.97% (2024), IonQ R&D prototype 99.99% (2025), Quantinuum H2 99.80% (2024), IBM Heron r2 99.70% (2024), IonQ Forte 99.60% (2022), IonQ Aria 99.50% (2022) and Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q 99.10% (2026).
quotes: Oxford Ionics (now IonQ) electronic-control gate 99.97% 2024 IonQ R&D prototype (electronic qubit control) 99.99% 2025

Quantinuum H2 (production) 99.80% 2024 IBM Heron r2 (ibm_kingston, 156Q) 99.70% 2024 IonQ Forte (36Q production) 99.60% 2022 IonQ Aria (25Q production) 99.50% 2022 Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q (production, Apr 2026) 99.10% 2026
assertions.certainty_reason: Reported values attributed to other work; the table does not give a measurement protocol.
assertions.reader_inference: The table is titled production hardware but its first two rows are research and prototype results. The years differ across rows (2022 to 2026), so rows are not measured under one protocol. The IonQ Forte and Aria figures are from 2022.

assertions.value: The authors claim that, for algorithms that require deep circuits, the higher-fidelity provider often produces useful results at fewer shots, partially offsetting the per-shot premium, and that deep circuits on the cheapest superconducting hardware may need more shots.
quotes: For algorithms that require deep circuits, the higher-fidelity provider often produces useful results at fewer shots, partially offsetting the per-shot premium.
so deep circuits may need more shots
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the paper gives no experiment or calculation for it.
assertions.reader_inference: The page prices no run with shots-to-solution, so the offset cannot be checked from its numbers. Table 3 compares cost for equal shot counts only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the VQE cost comparison illustrates the cost-vs-fidelity trade-off that determines hardware choice for variational workloads.
quotes: illustrating the cost-vs-fidelity trade-off that determines hardware choice for variational workloads
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's interpretation; no fidelity or convergence result is reported for VQE.
assertions.reader_inference: The VQE rows hold prices at equal iteration and shot counts and report no fidelity, convergence or solution-quality outcome, so the stated trade-off is not shown by the page's data.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum processors need specialised, low-utilisation infrastructure (dilution refrigerators near absolute zero for superconducting qubits, or ultra-high-vacuum ion traps and laser systems for trapped-ion machines), that each job occupies the device exclusively so providers meter access tightly, and that the result is a price span of more than 180x per shot between the cheapest and most expensive gate-model devices.
assertions.anchor: Section 8 FAQ (Why is quantum computing so expensive)
quotes: Quantum processors need specialised, low-utilisation infrastructure: dilution refrigerators near absolute zero for superconducting qubits, or ultra-high-vacuum ion traps and laser systems for trapped-ion machines.
Each job occupies the device exclusively, so providers meter access tightly, by shot, by QPU-minute or by monthly subscription.
The result is a price span of more than 180x per shot between the cheapest and most expensive gate-model devices
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's explanation with no cost data behind it.
assertions.reader_inference: The page gives no cost breakdown, so the causal link from infrastructure to price is asserted, not shown. Prices also reflect vendor choices that the page does not discuss.

assertions.value: The authors state that provider pricing pages are re-fetched every 90 days and that a pre-deploy gate blocks publication of any change containing a stale dated row. They report that the Braket figures were cross-checked against the AWS Price List API (publication 2026-08-31) and that IonQ Aria was confirmed withdrawn from the Braket device list.
quotes: Provider pricing pages are re-fetched every 90 days. The pre-deploy gate blocks publication of any change containing a stale dated row.
The Braket figures were also cross-checked against the AWS Price List API (publication 2026-08-31), and IonQ Aria was confirmed withdrawn from the Braket device list.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own verification procedure in Section 7.
assertions.reader_inference: A 90-day cadence means any price here can be up to about three months old at the time of reading, and the verification date is 2026-09-07.

assertions.value: The page is bylined Oliver Wakefield-Smith, Digital Signet, 3 June 2026, and states it is an independent reference with no affiliate revenue and no vendor sponsorships. Its footer gives a last-verified date of 2026-09-07.
assertions.anchor: Page header, Section on references, footer
quotes: Oliver Wakefield-Smith · Digital Signet · 3 June 2026
Independent reference. No affiliate revenue. No vendor sponsorships.
Last verified 2026-09-07
assertions.certainty_reason: A self-description by the page's publisher.
assertions.reader_inference: The source is a commercial-site reference page, not a peer-reviewed paper. It cites vendor pricing pages and press items and has one named author. The header date (3 June 2026) differs from the verification date (2026-09-07), so the byline date marks first publication and not the price snapshot.
